analysis.one_liner: Gives workers stronger tools to recover unpaid wages and imposes new pay-disclosure duties on employers.
analysis.headline: The bill had 33 Senate cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it easier for workers to recover wages their employers unlawfully withheld. It required employers to give workers written paystubs, disclose pay rates and job classifications at hire, and pay final wages within 14 days of leaving a job. It also raised penalties for wage violations, lengthened the time workers have to sue from 2-3 years to 4-5 years, tripled damages for willful violations, barred employers from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue in arbitration, and funded $50 million a year in grants for community groups that help workers file wage claims [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers fail to pay minimum wage, overtime, promised contract wages, or final paychecks. The bill's own findings note wage theft is estimated to cost workers more than $15 billion a year, with women, immigrants, and Black workers disproportionately affected, and 68 percent of surveyed low-wage workers reporting some form of wage theft in a recent workweek [S2]. Workers who keep tips would gain new penalties against employers who take them [S2]. Law-abiding employers would also gain a more level playing field against competitors who cut costs by not paying workers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Gives workers a federal right to recover the full wage their contract or union agreement promised, not just the legal minimum — the bill's findings note that under current law workers can often recover only minimum wage when an employer steals more [S2].

Requires employers to disclose pay rate, job classification, and overtime status within 15 days of hire and to provide itemized paystubs showing hours worked, rates, deductions, and tips — the bill's findings note there is currently no federal paystub requirement, which impedes detecting wage theft [S2].

Requires final paychecks within 14 days of leaving a job, with daily pay continuing for up to 30 days if the employer is late — the findings note federal law currently has no deadline for final pay at all [S2].

Raises the financial stakes for violators: liquidated damages rise from an equal amount to 2-3 times the stolen wages plus interest, civil fines rise to as much as $110,150 per affected employee for repeat or willful violations, and repeat offenders who falsify records must be referred to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution [S2].

Extends the time workers have to sue from 2 years (3 for willful violations) to 4-5 years, pauses that clock during Labor Department investigations, and lets courts presume the worker's own testimony about hours worked is accurate when the employer failed to keep records [S2].
Makes the right to sue in court non-waivable, so an employer cannot use a pre-dispute arbitration agreement to block a worker from joining a collective wage claim [S2].

Authorizes $50 million per year through fiscal 2027 in competitive grants so community organizations, unions, and legal aid groups can educate workers, collect evidence, and partner with the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division on enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who underpay workers, misclassify employees as exempt or as contractors, or keep tips — through higher fines, tripled damages, interest, and longer legal exposure. Compliant employers also bear new paperwork costs: written pay disclosures within 15 days of hire, itemized paystubs, and five-year record requests within 21 days of a worker's request [S2]. Taxpayers fund the $50 million annual grant program [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers violating wage laws, plus compliance costs

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new administrative burdens on every covered employer — initial and updated pay disclosures, detailed paystubs for all hourly workers, and a duty to hand over up to five years of payroll records within 21 days of a worker's request — costs that fall hardest on small businesses with limited payroll staff [S2].

By extending the statute of limitations to 4-5 years, allowing courts to presume a worker's testimony is accurate when records are incomplete, and barring employers from enforcing arbitration agreements for wage claims, the bill significantly increases litigation exposure, which honest supporters would acknowledge could raise legal costs even for employers who act in good faith [S2].
The bill authorizes $50 million in federal spending per year through fiscal 2027 for grant programs, a recurring taxpayer cost with no dedicated funding source [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and large: the bill's own findings estimate wage theft costs workers more than $15 billion a year and that current penalties are too weak to deter repeat offenders — one-third of employers caught stealing wages kept doing it [S2]. Against that, the costs are real but secondary: compliance paperwork for employers, higher litigation risk, and $50 million a year in grant spending [S2]. A fair reading is that the bill's costs fall mostly on employers who are violating the law already, while its paperwork and litigation costs also touch well-run businesses. The design is aggressive — treble damages, a 5-year lookback, and no arbitration waivers — but aimed at a documented enforcement failure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the session ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, joined by 32 cosponsors — 31 Democrats and Independent Bernie Sanders — with no Republican cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].

That was the bill's last action. The committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and no version passed either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on underpaying workers — or who would have faced higher fines, tripled damages, longer liability windows, and lost arbitration shields — are better off because the bill never advanced. The committee's inaction meant no member ever had to vote on it.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 32 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independent; a senior appropriator who could have used other vehicles but did not attach it to one.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: Senator (I), HELP Committee chair; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, he never scheduled a markup or hearing on it, so it never left committee.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it clear majority-party support on paper, but no committee action or floor vote followed.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its September 2023 referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 15 months of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the party's members offered no support as the bill sat without action.

against.name: Employer and business trade groups
against.what_they_did: Business lobbies historically oppose expansion of wage-and-hour damages, statute-of-limitations extensions, and arbitration limits; the congressional record here shows no activity on this bill, so any role in its demise is not documented in the provided sources.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely from the Democratic caucus: 31 Democrats plus one Independent sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no Republican joined [S3].

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, janitorial, construction, warehouses)
industries.note: These industries have the highest measured rates of wage-and-hour noncompliance, and the bill would hit them hardest: fines up to $110,150 per affected employee for repeat violations, tripled damages, a 4-5 year liability window, and mandatory criminal referral for record-falsifying repeat offenders [S2]. Their gain under the bill would come from paying workers what they already owe; their loss if it fails is the status quo continuing [S2].

industries.industry: Payroll processing and HR compliance providers
industries.note: New federal mandates for pay disclosures, itemized paystubs, and record requests would create demand for payroll and compliance services to handle the required disclosures and five-year record retention [S2].

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and subcontractors relying on worker misclassification
industries.note: The bill makes misclassification a named form of wage theft, requires employers to disclose the legal basis for classifying a worker as exempt, and exposes misclassification to the same doubled and tripled damages and fines [S2].

The bill bars enforcement of pre-dispute arbitration agreements for federal wage claims, removing a key defense employers use against collective wage suits, while creating more litigation overall [S2].
